# Outside the sheriff's office: did he know a gunman was behind the door?

## The short answer

**No. At the moment he first put his hand out to that door he had no idea there
was anyone behind it, let alone anyone holding a cocked gun.** He finds out only
when the door opens, and everything he does from that instant on is catching up
to a surprise.

## What actually happens, in order

* **≈476.3 s** — Cut to the street. A man in a light shirt and dark neckerchief
  rides in at an ordinary walk and pulls up at the hitching rail outside the
  sheriff's office.
* **≈478 s** — He steps down, unhurried.
* **≈479.5–480.8 s** — He loops the reins over the hitching rail and ties them,
  using both hands, head down, his back to the building.
* **≈481–483 s** — Cut inside. We (not he) see the trap: the man in the dark
  vest who has just held the sheriff at gunpoint and marched him into his own
  cell (≈461–476 s) crosses the office with a drawn revolver and drops down out
  of sight behind the desk, leaving the sheriff shut behind the bars.
* **≈483.0–484.2 s** — Cut back outside to the boardwalk. He walks the last
  couple of steps to the office door past the reward posters, arm already
  swinging out ahead of him, and takes hold of the door handle. Both hands are
  empty.
* **≈484.4–485.2 s** — The door gives, and he instantly ducks, doubles over and
  hurls himself bodily sideways out of the opening, fetching up flattened
  against the wall on the far side of the door frame.
* **≈485.5–486.0 s** — Only now does he drag his revolver out and thumb the
  hammer back.
* **≈486.6–487.6 s** — He leans out from behind the jamb and fires into the dark
  doorway; from ≈488 s the man behind the desk is firing back.

## The two things about his own behaviour that give it away

**1. His gun was still in its holster when he reached for that door — and the
hand he put on the latch was his gun hand.** Right through the approach
(≈483.0–484.2 s) both of his hands are plainly empty; the hand he stretches out
ahead of him is open and bare, and it is the same near-side hand he will be
shooting with a second and a half later. He does not draw before he touches the
door. He does not even rest his hand on his holster or hook a thumb in his belt
near it. He simply reaches out and takes the handle the way a man opens his own
front door — which means he deliberately committed his shooting hand to a
doorknob. The revolver does not appear until ≈485.5 s, *after* the dive is over
and he is already behind the wall. The sequence is reach → door opens → dive →
draw, and that last step is in exactly the wrong place for a man who knew. If he
had suspected a gun on the other side he would have had his own in his fist
before the latch ever moved.

**2. The whole approach was casual and unguarded — he rode in openly, dismounted
in plain view, and spent several unhurried seconds with his back to the building
tying his horse up with both hands.** He comes down the open street at a walk
rather than circling round the back; he gets down on the exposed street side of
the rail directly in front of the office; and then he stands there for four or
five seconds, head down and both hands occupied knotting his reins to the rail,
with the office door behind his shoulder. In all that time he never once looks
at the office, never checks the window, never glances at the rail to see whose
other horses are standing there, and never scans the street. Then he walks
straight on to the door and takes hold of it in one continuous movement — no
pause on the threshold to listen, no knock, no call-out, and no sidestep to put
himself clear of the opening; he is square on to the door, close up, looking
down at the latch. Every bit of that is the behaviour of a man running a routine
errand. A man who thought he was walking into a trap would not have pinned
himself in the open with both hands full of bridle reins first.

## A third confirmation: the dive itself

The way he goes sideways tells the same story. It is not a controlled,
pre-planned move — he does not stand off to one side and swing the door open at
arm's length the way you would if you expected a bullet through it. He is caught
standing right at the opening, upright and close in, still holding the handle,
and what follows is a scrambling, off-balance lunge: head down, body doubled
over and smeared with motion blur, hat pushed askew, clawing at his belt on the
way across. Only once he is safely behind the
solid wall does he straighten up, get the gun out, cock it and start returning
fire around the jamb. That is a startle reflex, not a tactic.

## Why the scene is built that way

This is straightforward dramatic irony. The film deliberately cuts inside during
the few seconds he is tying his horse, so that the audience watches the henchman
lock the sheriff in the cell and crouch down behind the desk with his gun out —
information the rider on the boardwalk never gets. The suspense of the shot
depends entirely on our knowing what he does not, and his relaxed, gun-holstered
walk up to that door is the thing that makes it work.
